articles.title: Death threats and isolation - the cost of fighting sexual violence in Iraq
articles.summary: Women say they share stories of abuse to highlight the issue, despite social pressure and safety fears.
articles.body:
This story contains details of sexual violence which some readers may find upsetting

"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him .

The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.

"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."

One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.

Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.

"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."

She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.

There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.

"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."

Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.

Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.

Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".

Amal - not her real name - has been battling in court for about five years. She accuses her ex-husband of repeatedly raping their daughter - who was under 18 at the time - at gunpoint.

She recalls her daughter's harrowing account of the incident, when she says the father walked into the girl's room and laid his weapon on her bed. She says he told her: "No-one will hear you if I kill you."

Sexual abuse has long been seen as a taboo subject in Iraq. I have been in touch with many survivors who say that they prefer to hush it up, because of a potential family backlash. Others told us they were afraid to go to the police, for fear of social stigma and possible harassment. But Amal was determined to seek justice and rushed to police to report the incident.

"She had lots of bruises around her wrists, as he held her hands tight. Whenever she tried to scream, he would cover her mouth with his hands," Amal says.

Amal showed me medical documents, including DNA evidence, which support her account.

A further demonstration of her ex-husband's cruelty came, Amal says, when she heard him tell a family member to "wash off our disgrace" if he was arrested. The expression is used in Iraq to refer to so-called honour killings - carried out in the belief that a woman has compromised a family's reputation.

Amal says she believes the father threatened to put an end to his daughter's life "so the medical report would not be released and the assault would not be proven".

She says her ex-husband is on the run and the court case remains open.

"I fought all alone," says Amal, bursting into tears as she says her ex-husband hired several lawyers but she could not afford legal representation, and her family turned a blind eye to the situation.

She no longer has any faith that a court ruling will come in her favour. "I just want him to stay out of my way forever," she says, with a sigh of despair.

Amal's daughter is more fortunate than some women who have experienced domestic sexual abuse in Iraq, as she has a safe place to live.

Many survivors have no independent income and nowhere to go. Iraq has very few shelters for abused women.

Those we know of were established by an organisation co-founded by Yanar Mohammed, an internationally recognised women's rights advocate. Last March she was murdered outside her house in Baghdad by armed men. The perpetrators are still unknown.

Experts working for the UN Human Rights Council wrote in April that Mohammed had been receiving death threats and online abuse for years, which were "believed to come from extremist religious militia".

Activists repeatedly told us that targeted attacks on their colleagues have been on the rise in recent years.

Hanaa Edwar, another prominent women's rights activist, says she saw Mohammed just two days before she was killed. She says she has also been threatened.

"There are no laws, no protection, and no justice for women in Iraq," she tells me.

"The problem in Iraq is not that women stay silent. It is that when they speak, very little in the system is built to listen, Mustafa Saadoon, head of the Iraqi Observatory for Human Rights, tells the BBC.

"A woman who reports sexual violence has to get past her family first, then a police station, then a court, and at every one of those doors someone is likely to tell her to settle it quietly."

Among the Iraqi women who say they feel failed by the system is Samira - not her real name.

She tells the BBC that walking in the street puts her on the edge, after repeated harassments.

Once, she says a man "was watching a porn movie on his phone and put it in my face" on public transport.

In another incident in Baghdad, she says a man once followed her in his car for over 10 minutes. "It was extremely upsetting... I saw a police car. I went over and told them what had happened. They said they didn't have the authority to do anything."

Although her mother is loving and supportive, Samira does not share any stories of sexual harassment with her. "If I tell my family, they will immediately ask me not to leave home in order to stay safe," she says.

She has lost faith in state institutions: "Many men, including police officers, find nothing wrong with sexual harassment. If you are not a harasser, you are not a man, this is how they see it," she adds.

Many women I spoke to in Iraq even accused police of sexual harassment. I put the accusation to Muqdad Miri, a spokesman for Iraq's interior ministry.

"Cases of harassment involving police personnel happen but they are very few. They get a very harsh punishment, up to 10 years in prison and are dismissed," says Miri.

I put it to him that some women were now documenting harassment on social media because they were afraid to report it to police. He said they were posting on social media because it was easier than filing an official report, and because doing so has become a common way to draw attention to a cause.

I also put to him Samira's experience, in which she says an officer told her that he had no authority to stop harassment. Miri said Samira could have filed a complaint against this officer.

There are no reliable statistics for sexual violence or harassment in Iraq. Miri told me that police have received about 300 reports of sexual violence since the beginning of the year. However, he accepts that the real number of cases is higher: "Many cases never reach the police because of society, customs and traditions."

The stories of the women the BBC spoke to draw a picture of their battle not just against sexual violence itself, but against deeply entrenched mentalities and social beliefs that allow it to persist.

Edwar has been advocating for women's causes for over 50 years and her assessment is gloomy: "Twenty-three years after Saddam Hussein's regime was brought down, it seems we are going backwards regarding women's rights."

But both she and Jassim say they refuse to give up: "If all of us are going to get scared, no-one will change anything," says Sarah.

If you have been affected by issues involving sexual abuse and violence, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line.

articles.title: Sense and Sensibility dance scene filmed at Penshurst Place
articles.summary: The Kent manor house features as a country dance location in the new film of Sense and Sensibility.
articles.body:
A medieval manor house in Kent can be seen in the latest cinematic adaptation of the Jane Austen novel Sense and Sensibility.

The Baron's Hall at Penshurst Place, near Tunbridge Wells, features as the location of a country hop dance scene with 150 actors, including Fiona Shaw and Daisy Edgar-Jones, and eight dogs.

Filming, which took place over the August Bank Holiday weekend last year, closed the historic house, Garden Tower and South Lawn to visitors.

Ben Thomas, general manager of the site, said they had enjoyed "two very intense days with a huge cast, huge crew, a lot of activity and a lot of fun and excitement".

The party scenes at Penshurst feature Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood, Esmé Creed-Miles as her sister Marianne, Caitríona Balfe as Mrs Dashwood, Fiona Shaw as Mrs Jennings, Frank Dillane as John Willoughby and Herbert Nordrum as Colonel Brandon.

"They were very good," added Thomas. "I didn't see any trips or falls, but it was a high energy, high excitement sort of dance."

About 150 members of crew worked on site to capture the action, setting up lighting rigs outside the building and a crane near the visitor entrance, suspending a powerful light high above the estate.

The film, which has been on release in cinemas since late September, features shots of the Baron's Hall corridor, the West Solar steps and entrances to the Inner Courtyard and King's Tower, as well as the Baron's Hall.

The hall was built in 1341 for Sir John de Pulteney, four-time Lord Mayor of London, and retains its 60ft (18.2m) high roof and central hearth.

Penshurst Place has featured in numerous TV and film productions over the years including Mary, Queen of Scots with Saoirse Ronan, Wolf Hall, The Princess Bride and Renegade Nell .

"We've been filming here since the '60s," said Thomas. "The Beverly Hillbillies had an episode filmed here back in the early '60s, Richard Burton filmed here for Anne of the Thousand Days.

"It's always exciting when a location manager chooses us for filming."

Penshurst Place is open to visitors until the end of October when it closes for winter.

articles.title: Red squirrel project opens £250k community grant
articles.summary: Groups from around northern England and southern Scotland can bid for funding to help the creatures.
articles.body:
Groups trying to protect red squirrels are being invited to bid for funding from a £250,000 pot.

The Red Squirrel Recovery Network (RSRN) said it hoped to "engage people from all backgrounds" with grants of up to £500 available for smaller activities to £5,000 to support ideas with a wider reach.

The project, which started in 2025 , works with conservation partners and volunteer groups across Northumberland, Cumbria, Manchester, Lancashire, Merseyside and southern Scotland to raise awareness of the endangered species.

In May, animal welfare group Save Our Reds said the species "still clings on" across Cumbria, Northumberland and the North Pennines but could disappear within 25 years.

Red squirrel populations across Britain have dramatically declined and have been estimated at about 287,000, the RSRN said.

According to Natural England , causes for the decline include the introduction of grey squirrels from the USA and Canada from 1876 spreading the squirrelpox virus, which is fatal to the red squirrels only.

Save Our Reds said habitat loss and weak enforcement of existing protections were adding to the problem.

Heather Harris, from the RSRN, said the project - which is funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund - aimed to "remind everyone of why red squirrels are so important to our heritage".

"There are many older generations who remember red squirrels, but we'd also would love to hear from younger people where nature isn't as accessible for them or who haven't had the experience of seeing red squirrels," she said.

The network said it wanted to support plans which helped local communities celebrate red squirrels and reconnect with nature, such as themed walks or improving spaces linked to conservation.

RSRN programme manager Mike Denbury said: "From introducing children to red squirrels for the very first time to delivering larger habitat protection projects, we're keen to hear your ideas on inspiring action for nature."

articles.title: River Tyne levels could release trapped nurdles downstream
articles.summary: Port of Tyne says it continues to monitor the nurdles in the River Tyne daily.
articles.body:
High river flows this autumn could flush 2.2 tonnes of microplastics downstream, scientists have warned.

Tonnes of the pellets, known as nurdles, were spilled into the River Tyne after a crash between two vessels at the Port of Tyne damaged two shipping containers.

According to new modelling from Newcastle University, about one in eight of the nurdles remained in the estuary six weeks after the spill.

The scientists have urged the authorities involved in the clean-up operation to use measures to intercept, trap or recover the nurdles before they move towards the North Sea.

Project lead Dr Matt Perks said: "Because river flows have been so low since July, pellets that moved up the estuary and were deposited have had little to move them on.

"When elevated river flows arrive, some of that material is likely to be flushed downstream, so now is the time to consider where it could be intercepted."

A temporary barrier was deployed in the water around the source of the spill three days after the incident in July.

Weeks after the spill, the microplastics were spotted more than 30 miles (48km) south of the source.

A spokesperson for Port of Tyne said recovery work has entered the next phase and they have taken responsibility for daily monitoring and collection.

Ambipar, its environmental response partner, finished its on-water activity on Sunday, but will provide specialist recovery support around the spring tides on 28 October and 9 November.

Director of place strategy at South Tyneside Council Stuart Wright said the multi-agency response group was "preparing" for the "additional movement of nurdles".

"It's important to remember that this is not unexpected and plans are in place to respond where required," he said.

The team at the university built a detailed computer model of the River Tyne and North Sea to track where the pellets have likely gone.

They said while the model provided an uncertain picture out at sea due to changing ocean currents and wind, the estuary findings were "robust".

Senior lecturer in physical geography Dr Seb Pitman said: "Our model reproduces the tide through the Tyne very closely, which gives us real confidence in what it says about the estuary itself."

Further modelling will take place over the coming weeks with the project, called Against the Flow, beginning fieldwork.

articles.title: North East paramedics experiment with AI note-taking tool
articles.summary: North East Ambulance Service is studying the effectiveness of AI in real-world patient interactions.
articles.body:
Paramedics are experimenting with the use of AI assistants in frontline services.

North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said it was in the middle of an eight-week trial studying the effectiveness of technology that records, transcribes and summarises patient conversations.

It said 38 individuals, ranging from paramedics to operational staff, were involved in the study and that it hoped the software may reduce staff workload.

The organisation's digital clinical lead Georgina Campbell said the trial would help the team better understand how emerging technology could be used "safely and effectively".

The AI tool works via the in-built iPad microphones used by ambulance staff, according to the NEAS, and is being used in real-world interactions between patients and paramedics.

All notes generated by the AI ambient voice technology, are reviewed and edited by a clinician before they are added to a patient's record, an NEAS spokesperson said.

The ambulance service said it had several hopes for the technology including the potential for it to improve record-keeping consistency and accuracy.

Campbell said: "This trial will help us understand how emerging technology can be used safely and effectively, while maintaining the high standards of care and record keeping that our patients and communities expect."

A spokesperson said the organisation would decide on the tool's future after the trial had concluded in November.

articles.title: Report reveals strain on fire crews tackling Langdale Moor blaze
articles.summary: Crews showed "exceptional commitment" during the fire on the North York Moors, the report states.
articles.body:
Fire crews faced significant pressure while tackling a moorland blaze which burned for 40 days, a report has found.

According to the report into North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service's performance and development, staff showed "exceptional commitment" during the blaze in the North York Moors National Park which started in early August 2025.

However, firefighters struggled to balance their work with their normal duties - including responding to other emergencies - and their other employment.

As a result of the report, the service has been recommended to develop better arrangements for relieving and rotating crews during lengthy incidents to protect staff welfare and maintain emergency cover.

The main blaze started at Langdale Moor on 11 August and at its height covered nearly 10 sq miles (25 sq km).

It was likely to have been caused by someone cooking using a campfire or gas burner, an investigation later found.

The report into the fire service's response, which is due to be considered by York and North Yorkshire Police, Fire and Crime Panel on Wednesday, said the blaze placed pressure on senior officers, full-time firefighters, on-call crews and volunteers.

"While on-call personnel demonstrated exceptional commitment throughout the response, sustained deployment began to affect primary employment commitments and operational availability," the report stated.

It also raised questions about expectations for firefighters to continue working beyond their normal shifts.

According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , the findings have come amid wider concerns about the availability of on-call firefighters across North Yorkshire, particularly in rural communities where fire stations rely heavily on personnel who have other jobs.

The report acknowledged that recruiting and retaining sufficient on-call firefighters remained a major challenge.

It also noted that employment commitments, training requirements and difficulties filling specialist roles all contributed to the problem.

Particular difficulties existed in recruiting qualified drivers and supervisory managers, with more than half of on-call supervisors also holding full-time firefighting contracts, the report found.

However, it added that recruitment was improving, with 53 new on-call firefighters joining so far this year, compared with annual intakes of between 32 and 34 in previous years.

But the report warned that new recruits required extensive training before becoming fully operational, meaning increased recruitment did not immediately translate into better emergency cover.

The service currently employs 306 full-time firefighters, 339 on-call firefighters and 14 volunteers, although some staff hold more than one role.

A review of future staffing requirements is under way, with the findings expected before the end of the year.

articles.title: Fly-tippers in Cornwall face £5k fine in new crackdown
articles.summary: Cornwall Council introduces new penalties after recording 17,500 incidents in five years.
articles.body:
Fly-tippers in Cornwall could face fines of up to £5,000 if they are caught illegally disposing waste.

The threat is a part of Cornwall Council's new push to quash the crime after it recorded 17,500 fly-tipping incidents in the past five years.

It has introduced the use of covert cameras to catch unlicensed waste carriers in the act, and is also encouraging residents to submit evidence if they catch anything on camera. Households who are found to have employed fly-tippers also face fines.

Cornwall Council said there was "no excuse" for the offence, and that it would hold fly-tippers to account.

"We work hard to identify those responsible for illegal dumping and will hold offenders to account wherever possible," said Sarah-Jane Brown, group leader for community protection at Cornwall Council.

"We're asking people to play their part and work with us to prevent fly-tipping, and to share any information that may help us trace those responsible for dumping rubbish."

Councillor Thalia Marrington, council cabinet member with responsibility for community safety and public protection, said: "Fly-tipping can cause serious harm to our communities, the environment and wildlife.

"It also costs councils and landowners huge amounts of money to clear up."

articles.title: Slow Horses leaves legacy at bowling alley and motorway services
articles.summary: Go Bowling in Dunstable still has the pink and yellow walls left by the production team.
articles.body:
Filming for television drama Slow Horses has helped provide improvements at a motorway service station and bowling alley.

Go Bowling in Dunstable, Bedfordshire, and Beaconsfield Services, on the M40 in Buckinghamshire, both featured in the fourth episode of the latest season of the Apple TV+ spy thriller which stars Sir Gary Oldman.

Motorway stop operator Extra MSA said income from the production would fund refurbishments to its grounds and facilities, including parking and landscaping.

In December 2024 , film crews redecorated the bowling venue for their scenes.

This included painting some of the walls pink and yellow, which owners liked enough to keep after the shoot ended.

James Brennan, a mechanic at the bowling alley who supervised filming, said: "When they came in, they said they were going to paint it pink and yellow and I said absolutely not, that sounds horrendous.

"But when they put it up, it looks great actually. The consensus of all the customers is that they liked it as well, so we kept it."

Brennan described the crew as a "well-oiled machine", adding that they used "a bit of trickery" to make two separate split corridors look like one continuous hallway on screen.

Weeks before arriving at the bowling alley, cast and crew filmed inside Beaconsfield Services and its car park.

Operations director Ross Mendenhall said hosting the filming was a "really exciting experience".

"Watching the scale of activity involved in bringing a production of this size to life was fascinating," he said.

"The cast and crew were a pleasure to work with and worked closely with us to minimise disruption for our customers throughout the process."

Season six of the programme hit screens last month and the latest episode was available from Wednesday.

articles.title: On Christmas Eve 2018, cracks forced residents from Sydney’s Opal Tower; after nearly eight years of repairs, relocations, a class action and two legal cases, the complex has been declared defect-free
articles.summary: Sydney’s Opal Tower has been declared defect-free nearly eight years after structural cracks forced residents to leave their homes on Christmas Eve 2018.
articles.body: Sydney’s Opal Tower has been declared defect-free nearly eight years after structural cracks forced residents to leave their homes on Christmas Eve 2018. What began as an emergency evacuation at the newly built residential complex led to years of repairs, temporary relocations, compensation efforts and legal disputes. According to ABC News, which reported the development, the building’s owners corporation marked the milestone at a ceremony following the extensive rectification work. A New South Wales Parliament inquiry report and the Supreme Court of NSW’s records provide the official background to the building’s defects and the class action that followed.Christmas Eve cracks triggered an evacuationThe Opal Tower, a 36-storey residential building at Sydney Olympic Park, became the focus of an emergency response on December 24, 2018, after cracks appeared in its structure. Residents were evacuated as authorities assessed whether the building was safe. The incident forced thousands of people to evacuate and raised wider concerns about construction quality in Australia’s apartment sector.The damage was not confined to a single visible crack. Further cracking was identified in the days that followed, prompting continued inspections and investigations. The New South Wales Government commissioned a technical investigation into what had gone wrong. Its findings pointed to construction and material deficiencies that required significant rectification work before the building could be considered safe. The incident also drew attention to the responsibilities of developers, builders, engineers and regulators when serious defects emerge in recently completed residential buildings.Repairs and relocations continued for yearsGetting residents back into their homes took time. While some apartments were cleared for reoccupation relatively quickly, others remained uninhabitable months after the evacuation. The New South Wales Parliament’s report on building standards and disputes recorded that 170 apartments were still uninhabitable in June 2019. By September that year, most residents had returned, although some were still waiting to move back.The repair process involved extensive work to address the structural problems identified during investigations. Owners and residents also had to deal with the practical consequences of relocation, including uncertainty about when they could return and how the defects would be resolved. The building’s recovery therefore extended far beyond the initial emergency. Years of rectification work and negotiations were needed before the owners corporation could announce the latest milestone.A class action and two legal casesThe aftermath also unfolded in court. The Supreme Court of New South Wales records the class action Terry Williamson v Sydney Olympic Park Authority, filed in 2019. The proceedings formed part of the efforts by apartment owners to pursue accountability and address the consequences of the building’s defects. The court’s case page lists the class action as completed, with a settlement approved.The class action was not the only legal dispute linked to Opal Tower. ABC News’ report describes two legal cases among the developments that followed the evacuation and years of rectification. These proceedings added to the complexity of resolving the building’s problems, as the parties involved faced questions about responsibility, repair costs and compensation. For owners, the legal process was closely tied to the wider effort to restore confidence in their homes and resolve the financial consequences of the incident.Opal Tower declared defect-freeOn October 10, 2026, ABC News reported that Opal Tower’s owners corporation had declared the building defect-free at a ceremony marking the completion of the rectification process. The report quoted owners corporation chairman Shady Eskander, who said the rectification work had involved consultants, the builder and others connected with the building’s design and construction.The report also said owners had been compensated and the legal matters resolved. A 20-year structural warranty was another part of the building’s position following the repairs. The declaration marks a significant change for a complex that became widely associated with structural cracking and questions about building standards. It also comes amid broader scrutiny of construction quality and regulation in New South Wales, issues examined in the Parliament’s inquiry into building standards, quality and disputes.A long road from evacuation to resolutionThe declaration does not erase the disruption that began on Christmas Eve 2018. Residents faced an abrupt evacuation, months of uncertainty for some households, lengthy repair work and legal proceedings before the building reached this point. Nearly eight years later, Opal Tower’s reported defect-free status represents the culmination of those efforts. The episode remains a prominent example of how serious defects in a newly completed residential building can affect residents well beyond the initial discovery, with repairs, relocations, compensation and legal disputes extending over years.You use AI every day. articles.title: #81: Your body doesn't stop working with age. It stops listening
articles.summary: When did you last play something so hard you were gasping for air and still grinning?
articles.body: When did you last play something so hard you were gasping for air and still grinning? Maybe a game of badminton, cricket or soccer, or chasing a child around the park. I don’t mean a workout. I mean play.For many adults, the honest answer is years ago. We tell ourselves that is simply what getting older looks like. The body slows, muscle fades, blood sugar creeps up, and we file it all under age. I no longer think it is that simple. At 54, I have more muscle, denser hips (hips don’t lie!) and less visceral fat than I had in my forties. Aging didn’t reverse, but my body moved in the opposite direction from what the calendar would predict. In today’s post (#81), I get into two scientific ideas that helped me understand why: insulin resistance and anabolic resistance.Before I get into the topic, I would like to announce the 6th cohort of the 28-day challenge that begins on October 4th. If you are interested in signing up for it, go to Deadline to sign up for this cohort is October 1st.What is insulin resistance?Insulin is a messenger. After a meal, it tells your muscle, liver and fat cells what to do with the nutrients arriving, including helping muscle and fat pull glucose out of the bloodstream. In insulin resistance, the cells respond less effectively, so the pancreas compensates by producing more insulin to get the same job done. For years that compensation can keep blood glucose looking fairly normal, which is why insulin resistance so often goes unnoticed. Eventually, the pancreas can’t keep up and blood glucose rises.Think of a doorbell. If nobody answers, you ring harder and longer. The bell works perfectly well. The house has simply stopped listening.What is anabolic resistance?Muscle has its own version of the same problem. Protein supplies the amino acids, and lifting something heavy supplies a powerful signal telling muscle to repair and build. Scientists measure part of that response as muscle protein synthesis. As we age, muscle tends to respond less to the same meal, and that blunted response is called anabolic resistance. At 25 you can whisper “build” and your muscles hear you, while at 65 you may need to speak much louder.The encouraging part is that older muscle still responds remarkably well when you do speak louder, especially when resistance exercises and enough protein are combined. Age may turn down the sensitivity of the receiver, but exercise turns up the signal.Are insulin and anabolic resistance connected?They aren’t the same biological process, but they overlap a great deal. Skeletal muscle is one of the body’s main destinations for glucose after a meal, so healthy, active muscle matters enormously for blood sugar control. The same things that make muscle less responsive to insulin, particularly inactivity and poor metabolic health, also blunt its response to protein.One experiment really brought this home for me. Researchers took healthy older adults and cut their activity to around 1,400 steps a day for just two weeks. In that short time, their muscle-building response to a meal fell by 26%, their insulin sensitivity after meals fell by 43%, and they measurably lost lean mass in their legs. In another study, a single night without sleep reduced muscle protein synthesis after a meal by about 18% in healthy young adults.The message isn’t that aging doesn’t matter, because it clearly does. It is that age isn’t acting alone. Its partners are movement, nutrition, metabolic health and sleep, and all of those are things we can change.My body has been my experimentMy story started in 2015, when a coronary calcium score of 266 at age 43 told me I had coronary artery disease, despite being lean and playing soccer regularly. That result changed how I thought about health, and I started measuring. Here is what eleven years of those measurements show. I started tracking muscle in December 2018, so that comparison covers about seven and a half years.The triglyceride-to-HDL ratio is an imperfect but useful clue that tracks with insulin resistance in many populations, and mine fell from 7.0 to 0.6. My HbA1c fell too, from 6.1% to 5.7%, but 5.7% still sits right at the threshold used to define prediabetes, so that one remains a work in progress. On the body composition side, I added 7.7 pounds of skeletal muscle while losing 7.1 pounds of fat between my late forties and mid fifties, and my hip bone density went up rather than down.This is an experiment with a sample size of one, so I don’t present it as scientific proof. But it makes the science very real to me. My age went up, my muscle went up, my fat went down and my hip bones got denser.Does this concept extend beyond muscle and insulin?It does, and bone is a wonderful example. Bone is living tissue whose cells sense mechanical load and adapt to it. In the LIFTMOR trial, postmenopausal women with low bone mass did supervised heavy resistance and impact training twice a week for eight months. Their bone density improved compared with women who didn’t train that way. My DEXA scans tell a similar personal story.Blood vessels respond in much the same way. Increased blood flow stimulates the lining of our arteries, and regular aerobic exercise improves how well arteries widen, even in older adults.Leptin is a hormone made by your fat cells. Think of it as a message to your brain saying, “We have enough energy stored, so you don’t need to keep eating.” But in obesity, even though leptin levels are often high, the brain may stop responding properly to the message. This is called leptin resistance. We know it happens, but we still don’t fully understand why it happens or how easily it can be reversed.The broader principle is simpler and easier to defend. Our bodies adapt to what we repeatedly ask them to do, and just as surely to what we stop asking them to do.What moved my numbers?Lifting two to three times a week. I lift heavy enough that the last few repetitions are genuinely difficult. A lifting session also makes muscle more responsive to protein for up to a day afterward, which is one of the best arguments I know for pairing strength training with protein consumption.Protein per meal, not just per day. Older muscles need a bigger dose at one sitting to switch on building, often around 30 to 40 grams, so I pay attention to each meal and not just the daily total. I average around 100 grams a day.Movement between workouts. That two-week step study stays with me because it shows how quickly inactivity takes its toll. I walk during calls, walk after meals and play soccer. Movement isn’t something I save for the gym.Cardio at different intensities. Comfortable aerobic work and harder intervals provide different stimuli, and both improve how my body handles sugar and how my arteries respond.Sleep. I went from around five hours a night to almost six. It remains my weakest link and the thing I am always working on improving.None of this is exotic, and that is exactly the point. They are just simple lifestyle changes I made consistently over a long time. The above changes are part of the 33 habits from my playbook. If you’d like to see all 33 habits, click on My Playbook. In fact, we are launching the 6th cohort of our 28-day challenge, where we introduce one habit each week, explain the science simply and help you make it stick, while keeping it fun. Longevity Circle community embers told us it became the starting point for transforming their health. By Day 28, it no longer feels like a program. It is simply how you live. If you are interested, sign up for the October 4th cohort by tomorrow's deadline (October 1st) at try28.comSo what is the takeaway?There is an old line, often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, though the attribution is shaky: we don’t stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing. Whoever said it, the thought captures something I increasingly believe. Aging changes our bodies, and none of us can exercise our way back to 25. But aging is not acting alone. Muscle and bone respond to load, insulin sensitivity responds to movement, blood vessels respond to exercise, and nutrition and sleep shape how well we adapt to all of it. Doing these doesn’t mean one has reversed aging. It tells us something far more useful: the aging body remains remarkably adaptable. We cannot stop getting older, but we can keep giving our bodies reasons to stay capable.If you want help figuring out where to start, join us in The Longevity Circle community at always, I would love to hear your thoughts and experiences in the comments.Author: Nickhil Jakatdar is the CEO of GenePath Diagnostics and the founder of PreventiveHealth.ai, working to make advanced diagnostics and credible health guidance more accessible, affordable, and actionable. articles.title: Ben Affleck says his kids rate his parenting below Jennifer Garner's: Why children may see co-parenting differently
articles.summary: Ben Affleck laughed that his kids don’t rate his parenting as highly as he’d hoped.
articles.body: Ben Affleck laughed that his kids don’t rate his parenting as highly as he’d hoped. He says he thinks he’s about “75 per cent as good” as his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner, but his three kids see it differently and put him at “40 per cent”. Talking about this, he spoke warmly about the respect he and Garner have for each other as they raise their children together.In his Sunday TODAY interview with Willie Geist, the 54-year-old actor spoke warmly about his ex-wife, Jennifer Garner. He called her a wonderful mother to their three children, Violet, 20, Seraphina, 17, and Samuel,14, whom they co-parent, and joked that she often leaves him feeling he is falling a little short.He then shared some lighthearted family maths. Affleck says he tells his kids, "75 per cent as good as your mom". The kids, he says, have a different number in mind, which is quite a bit lower, "Maybe 40 per cent," according to Affleck, who laughed it off and gave himself a B plus.Behind the jokes, he spoke seriously about gratitude and respect. The former couple shares custody on a week-on, week-off schedule, and he says he plans his work around being close to his children.This brings us to the question of why children rate their two parents so differently.Let us see what research has to say on this.Mothers and fathers often parent differentlyAccording to a 2008 study by Cliff McKinney and Kimberly Renk in the Journal of Family Issues, mothers and fathers often use different parenting styles, and older teens and young adults judge each parent separately. The study says that these views affect the young person's emotional adjustment and also suggests that having at least one authoritative parent, meaning one who is both caring and firm, can act as a protective factor. So when kids rate one parent lower, it may be a representation of different roles and habits, not a failing grade.Conduct of parents after divorce also impacts children’s emotional wellbeingA 2020 study in Clinical Psychology Review researched 115 groups of divorced families, covering 24,854 families in total. It found that when former partners keep fighting, and when parenting is harsh or unsupportive, children are more likely to struggle with their emotions and behaviour. The researchers also found that the way parents treat their children helps explain why this happens. But even though the individual effects were small, how parents treat their kids and each other seems to matter more than who is the "better" parent.Watching parents get alongA 2020 meta-analysis, published in Psychological Bulletin, reviewed 169 studies on children's emotional and behavioural difficulties. It found that the quality of the parents' relationship and the way they handle conflict highly impact how children fare, and many of these had a lasting impact over time. This can explain why Affleck's words about respect for his ex-partner show a lot about healthy co-parenting when he talked about mutual respect with Garner and said he is grateful to her.You use AI every day. articles.title: New Yorkers queued for hours to buy discarded subway hardware at an MTA sale where old signs cost $500 to over $1,000, orange seats sold for about $900 and Spike Lee picked up a Penn Station sign
articles.summary: New Yorkers waited for hours in south Brooklyn to buy old subway signs, plastic seats and other items removed from the city's transit system at an annual
articles.body: New Yorkers waited for hours in south Brooklyn to buy old subway signs, plastic seats and other items removed from the city's transit system at an annual sale organised by the Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) on Sunday.The two-day sale connected to New York's subway system offered station signs, seats and MetroCards, many of which had once been part of everyday journeys across the city. According to a report by news agency AFP, around 4,000 people attend the event each year.While some signs were priced at more than $1,000, the familiar orange subway seats were sold for around $900 each. Among the shoppers was also filmmaker Spike Lee, who bought a metal sign bearing the name of Penn Station.The sale took place at an open-air market in south Brooklyn, where visitors queued for hours before being allowed inside. To give everyone an opportunity to look through the available items, organisers limited each shopper to 45 minutes. Once their time was over, other visitors could enter and search for what they wanted.Although New York's subway is often criticised for being noisy, dirty and sometimes affected by flooding, many residents still have a strong connection with it.Old subway signs fetch hundredsAmong those searching for a particular item was 61-year-old Nori Juba, who managed to find a large sign displaying the name of Grand Central station. The sign also carried the numbers of the subway lines he uses every day.Juba acknowledged that the city's subway system has its problems. He described it as "old and creaky and it's outdated," but said those qualities were also part of its appeal."But I think that's what makes it interesting. And this piece of metal is dirty. It smells like a subway station, but there's something about it that makes it real New York, one of a kind in the world," he said.Such items do not come cheaply. A medium-sized subway sign was priced at around $500, while larger signs could cost more than $1,000. The orange plastic seats commonly seen inside New York subway trains were selling for approximately $900 each.Despite the prices, shoppers continued to turn up, hoping to find something associated with their favourite stations or daily journeys.Spike Lee buys Penn Station signThe sale attracted filmmaker and New York resident Spike Lee, who was seen meeting shoppers and posing for photographs.Lee bought a metal sign marked Penn Station, a subway stop associated with Madison Square Garden, where his favourite basketball team, the New York Knicks, plays its home games.Speaking to reporters, Lee recalled using the subway regularly while growing up in New York. Although he no longer takes the train to major basketball games, he said he had always paid for his journeys.He also joked about his record as a passenger, saying, "I never jumped the turnstile either. Let the record state!"The story behind the MTA saleThe Metropolitan Transportation Authority has sold old subway signs to collectors for years. However, the decision to allow members of the public to browse and purchase the items in person came more recently.Paul Dvoskin, the director responsible for the programme, said the idea developed around five years ago. "Five years ago, an idea was born to hold a garage sale of sorts, and to let people just come in and purchase these items" in person, he explained.The organisers initially called the event a grab-and-go sale, but the response exceeded their expectations. "We called it a grab-and-go back then, and it just ended up being significantly more popular than we ever thought it would be."Subway seats and MetroCards in demandAccording to the organisers, the orange plastic subway seats have become particularly popular since they were introduced for sale last year.Another item attracting attention is the MetroCard, the small yellow magnetic card long associated with travel on New York's public transport system. The cards have recently been retired from use and were available at the sale for $6 each.Not everyone arrived with hundreds of dollars to spend. Trinyce and Ijeoma, two women in their twenties, came with a combined budget of $70 and hoped to find something suitable for decorating their apartment.For Ijeoma, the purpose was to bring something connected to the city into her home. "I'd like a piece of New York to represent my living space, like as a representation of me," she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
